q-335054.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-2x(t)+3,\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
$[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ {{field-1}}
$\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$
q-335054.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+3 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+3 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hint: eAt=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)], where A=[0440].

EXPLANATION

Writing our system in matrix form, we get x′(t)=[0440]x(t)+g(t), where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)] and g(t)=[04]. So, the matrix of the system is A=[0440].

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)⏟homogeneous part+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds⏟particular solution, where x(t0) is the initial condition vector.

Let's evaluate each part separately:

  • First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that eAt=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)]. Since the initial conditions are given at t=t0=0, we have eA(t−t0)=eAtx(0)=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)][00]=[00].

  • Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that eA(t−s)=[cosh⁡(4(t−s))sinh⁡(4(t−s))sinh⁡(4(t−s))cosh⁡(4(t−s))]. So, we have eA(t−s)g(s)=[cosh⁡(4(t−s))sinh⁡(4(t−s))sinh⁡(4(t−s))cosh⁡(4(t−s))][04]=[4sinh⁡(4(t−s))4cosh⁡(4(t−s))]. Thus, we obtain ∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds=∫0t[4sinh⁡(4(t−s))4cosh⁡(4(t−s))]ds=[−cosh⁡(4(t−s))−sinh⁡(4(t−s))]s=0s=t=[cosh⁡(4t)−1sinh⁡(4t)].

Finally, we get x(t)=[00]+[cosh⁡(4t)−1sinh⁡(4t)]=[cosh⁡(4t)−1sinh⁡(4t)].

q-335401.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

q-335401.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$ and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L4}$ we have

$$
y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Using $y(0)=x(0)$ from $\text{L5}$, this becomes

$$
y(t)-x(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s,
$$

so

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substituting $y(0)=x(0).$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L9}.$ From $\text{L8}$ we know that

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).
$$

Substituting ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$ into

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s
$$

from $\text{L7}$ gives

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Therefore, $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by $\text{substituting }{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).$

Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

q-335404.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{e}^{At}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)
$$

from $\text{L1}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-At}x(t) \\  & =x(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$

Question 5

Consider the inhomogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(0) is presented below.

L1: Let y(t)=e−Atx(t)

L2: y′(t)=−Ae−Atx(t)+e−Atx′(t)

L3: y′(t)=e−Atg(t)

L4: y(t)−y(0)=∫0te−Asg(s)ds

L5: y(0)=x(0)

L6: y(t)=x(0)+∫0te−Asg(s)ds

L7: eAty(t)=eAtx(0)+∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

L8: eAty(t)=x(t)

L9: x(t)=eAtx(0)+∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

substituting x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)

EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L2 and L3. Starting from y′(t)=−Ae−Atx(t)+e−Atx′(t) in L2 and substituting x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t) from the original system gives
    y′(t)=−Ae−Atx(t)+e−At(Ax(t)+g(t))=−Ae−Atx(t)+Ae−Atx(t)+e−Atg(t)=e−Atg(t). Thus, L3 follows from L2 by substituting x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).

  • Next, we consider lines L6 and L7. Multiplying both sides of y(t)=x(0)+∫0te−Asg(s)ds from L6 by eAt gives
    eAty(t)=eAtx(0)+eAt∫0te−Asg(s)ds=eAtx(0)+∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds. Therefore, L7 follows from L6 by multiplying both sides by eAt.

  • Finally, we consider lines L1 and L8. Multiplying both sides of y(t)=e−Atx(t) from L1 by eAt gives
    eAty(t)=eAte−Atx(t)=x(t). Therefore, L8 follows from L1 by multiplying both sides by eAt.
